concepts.def: Runs from 0 to 14 — measures acidity or alkalinity
A solution with pH below 7 — releases H⁺ ions
Solution with pH above 7 — releases OH⁻ ions
Changes colour through the rainbow with pH
Strong fully ionises; weak only partly ionises

walkthroughs.body_html:
pH runs from 0 to 14.

Below 7 = acidic. Exactly 7 = neutral. Above 7 = alkaline.

The lower the pH, the more H⁺ ions. The higher the pH, the more OH⁻ ions.

Each step on the scale is a 10× change in H⁺ concentration.

Litmus: red in acid, blue in alkali.

Universal indicator: red (strong acid) → orange/yellow → green (neutral) → blue → purple (strong alkali).

Phenolphthalein: colourless in acid/neutral, pink in alkali.

A strong acid fully ionises in water — every molecule gives up its H⁺. Examples: HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃.

A weak acid only partly ionises — most molecules stay intact. Examples: ethanoic acid, citric acid.

For the same concentration, strong acids have a lower pH than weak acids.

mcqs.q: What is the pH of a neutral solution?

options: Ethanoic acid
Citric acid
Hydrochloric acid (HCl)
Carbonic acid

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid?
options: A strong acid fully dissociates in water; a concentrated acid has a high amount of acid per volume — these are independent properties.
A strong acid is one that has been heated to higher temperature.
Enantiomers are the same molecule drawn differently on paper.
Strong and concentrated mean the same thing for acids.

mcqs.q: When an acid neutralises an alkali, what is the pH of the resulting solution?
options: Approximately 7 if equivalent amounts of strong acid and strong alkali react — but it varies with strength.
A strong acid is one that has been heated to higher temperature.
Neutralisation always produces a solution with pH 0.
Neutralisation always produces a solution with pH exactly 7 regardless of the acid and base used.

mcqs.q: What is the relationship between two enantiomers?
options: Enantiomers are the same molecule drawn differently on paper.
Enantiomers have different boiling points and react completely differently with all reagents.
Neutralisation always produces a solution with pH 0.
They are non-superimposable mirror images that rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions but have identical chemical and physical properties otherwise.
